title: Krishna Reveals His Divine Form
story:
Inside the prison cell of Mathura, a newborn lay in his father's arms. He was moments old, small and new to the world — and then, in an instant, he was far more than that.

Still lying where he had been born, the child took on a form no infant could take. Four arms; eyes like lotus petals; and in his hands the conch, the discus, the mace, and the lotus. A crown of precious stone rested on his head, bright earrings hung from his ears, and his hair fell around him in a thousand shining locks. Vasudeva looked down, and wonder filled his face, for he understood at last whom he was holding. He bowed his head, folded his hands, and began to praise the Lord he held as his own son.

He spoke of how the whole world rises from this child and rests in him again; of the three colors the child wears — the white that preserves, the red that creates, the dark that brings an age to its end; of how he sets the three worlds in motion by his own power and is never touched by the changes he sets in motion. The child could not be known through the senses, Vasudeva said, only through a quiet and discerning mind — and he had come down into his own house to protect the world. Then his praise turned to fear. Kamsa, Devaki's own brother, the king who ruled Mathura, had already killed every child born before this one, and even now, hearing of this birth, he might be coming with weapons in his hands.

Devaki too looked on the child, and she knew him. She praised him as the light that cannot be seen, the changeless witness behind all change, the lamp that lights the soul itself, the refuge of everyone who is afraid. But her fear was sharper than her husband's. “May that wicked one never learn of your birth,” she said. “Save us from the terrible son of Ugrasena. Hide this extraordinary form, O soul of the universe, before he finds us.”

Then the child answered them, in a voice that was an infant's and something older than the world. He spoke of a time long before this life, when the two of them had been a childless couple, set by Brahma to bring children into the world. They had turned away from every worldly pleasure, and through rain and wind and heat and cold they had performed long and terrible penances, living on fallen leaves and on air, their minds held still. At the end of it he had appeared to them and offered a boon — and they, seeing no one in all the world to equal him in character or in generosity, had asked for a son like himself. He had granted it.

Then he told them the rest. He had been born to them once in that first life, and again, later, as the son of Aditi, born of Kashyapa. Now, in this third birth, he had come to them once more, with the same form, and he had shown it to them so that they would remember: their long penance, the boon, and the many times they had known him as child and as Lord. “You have known me,” he said, “as your son and as the divine, again and again.”

Then, having spoken, he let the dazzling form withdraw. The four arms were gone, the crown and the earrings and the thousand shining locks. In Vasudeva's arms lay an ordinary infant again, quiet and small. And his parents held him, and understood that the child they had been given was also the one who had chosen them — not once, but three times.
reflection: The Lord's words do the work that the splendor only begins: he reminds his parents that their son is also their Lord, and that their love for him is not new but very old. What looks like a miracle of light resolves into a quieter truth, remembrance.
tradition_note: The Vishnu Purana (5.3) folds this revelation into the moment of the birth itself; the Bhagavata Purana tells it as the child's own speech to his parents.
next_story_tease: But the child could not stay in the prison; before dawn, Vasudeva would have to carry him across the river.
hero_scene: The newborn Krishna revealing a four-armed form, conch, discus, mace and lotus in his hands, crowned and radiant, as Vasudeva and Devaki bow before him in the prison cell.
